text: find and union with path compression.
each set is a tree; the root (green) names the set

Union-find (并查集 , disjoint set union) keeps items split into groups and answers two questions fast: find "which group is x in?" and union "merge the groups of x and y". Each group is a tree stored in a parent[] array; the root represents the group.
Path compression: while finding the root, point every node on the way straight at the root. After that, operations are almost O(1) each.
Yes Yes No

Relatives are a union-find on people (P1551). To connect g separate groups you need exactly g − 1 more roads, and every successful union lowers g by one (P1536). Family trees with names use map<string, string> as the parent array (P2814).

"The enemy of my enemy is my friend": give each person i a second node i + n meaning "i's enemies", and unite a with b + n, b with a + n (P1892). Checking constraints in the right order, equalities first, uses the same tool after compressing big numbers (P1955).
String hashing and the unordered containers.

A hash turns a key (a number, a string) into a small index, so the key can be stored in or looked up from an array slot directly. Different keys may land on the same index (a collision); a good hash makes that rare, and a hash table keeps a short list per slot.
abc aaaa abc abcc

Read the string as a number in base 131 and let unsigned long long overflow, which is arithmetic mod 264. Equal strings always get equal hashes; different strings almost never do. Then count distinct values with sort + unique (P3370).
A hash compares fingerprints, not the strings themselves: a collision gives a wrong answer silently. Use a large base and mod 264 (or two different hashes) to make it practically impossible.

Keep the first copy of each number: print it only if it was not seen before (P4305). Use the hash containers when order does not matter and speed does.
set and map in practice: nearest values and records.

set keeps distinct values sorted; map keeps (key, value) pairs sorted by key. Besides insert, find and erase in O(log n), they answer "nearest value" questions with lower_bound , which a hash table cannot do.

Key points to memorise
1. Union-find: parent[x] = x at start; find the root; union = point one root at the other.
2. Path compression: parent[x] = find(parent[x]).
3. g groups need g − 1 links; each successful union lowers g by 1.
4. Enemies: extra node i + n means "i's enemies".
5. String hash: h = h × 131 + c in unsigned long long (mod 2⁶⁴).
6. Hash containers: O(1) average, unordered; set/map: O(log n), sorted.
7. Nearest value in a set: lower_bound and the element before it.
8. map[key] creates a missing key; use count() to test, erase() returns how many removed.
